utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First I would like to say good morning to the interpreters in the booths. Good morning. We can be sure that everybody can hear me, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused, my colleagues, and now we are going to continue. It is now a quarter after 10, Mr. Kehoe. You have until a quarter to 11. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Okay, we can now have General Marin brought in, that is the witness. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you that this is a public hearing. Before we begin, I would like to welcome Joelle Sauvage, who is a French legal officer who is the presiding Judge of the Appeals Chamber, and I would like to thank the parties and my colleagues as well for having agreed to her having come here. She has been a Judge for a long time, I'm not going to say how long, because it is a woman, it wouldn't be proper. All right, I would like to thank you. All right, Brigadier, Marin, the floor is yours, did you rest up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President, thank you for asking me, and good day to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, given that we have a half-hour, I would like to expedite our way through some of these issues. If I can just take the Court, based on the documents that the Brigadier reviewed yesterday, and specifically referring to Article 27, again, of Exhibit 533, excuse me, Exhibit 534, which is the decree on the military district courts. If I may read through this, Mr. President, and give the documents to the Court and move on with the questioning, it would speed things up significantly. In Article 27, the third paragraph that notes concerning the powers of a commander to arrest; it notes that a military commander at the position of the commander of the regiment, or at a hierarchically equivalent or higher position, as well as authorised officials of the internal affairs and security bodies and military police, may arrest a person in the military in cases provided for by the Law on Criminal Procedure and ordered custody. If I might have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this in, number 2, 27? This is tab 2, but there are several texts; could you tell me which one this is, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are referring to Exhibit 534, the decree on military courts, and we are discussing the accused's power to arrest within the decree on military courts in Article 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, all right, my eminent colleague, Judge Riad, has given it to me. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This cross references, Mr. President, the Law on Criminal Procedure and ordered custody, and I'm referring to Article 191 in that decree.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The following document is 537, 537A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Article 91 of Exhibit 537, Your Honours, says, "Custody shall always be ordered against a person if there is a warranted suspicion that he has committed a crime for which the law prescribes the death penalty." Excuse me, I'm sorry, the transcript says Article 91, and it should read Article 191 in Exhibit 537, and that notes that "Custody shall always be ordered against a person if there is a warranted suspicion that he has committed a crime for which the law prescribes the death penalty. Custody need not be ordered if the circumstances indicate that in the particular case involved the law prescribes a less severe penalty may be pronounced. And the reference point is back to Article 41 of the criminal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to determine those crimes for which the death penalty is called for. And for that point I would like to go to the criminal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which is the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 538, 538A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this particular exhibit, Mr. President and Your Honours, this is the law from the criminal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which talks about those crimes for which mandatory custody is warranted. And these crimes, as the Court can review in the particular statutes that are set forth in Exhibit 538, include crimes of genocide, crimes against the civilian population, the wounded and the sick, prisoners of war, murder of the enemy who surrender their arms, et cetera; those crimes account for many of the crimes that we are discussing or have been discussing in this trial. So, with those particular references, Mr. President, Your Honour, we will continue to examine the witness on the remaining subjects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, in addition to the powers that we discussed previously concerning the accused's power to arrest and investigate, I would like to show you two exhibits, and those are Exhibit 456/74 and Prosecutor’s Exhibit 456/77. Now, Brigadier, the first order, 456/74 is an order of the accused, Colonel Blaskic, by packet on the 24th of October 1992, and it reads as follows: "Mensud Alic, mayor of the JNA, is currently in Trogir. If he should take the road to Travnik, arrest him; and if he resists, execute him." That's Exhibit 456/74. The next exhibit, 456/77 is in October of 1993, almost a year later, and this is the 11th of October, 1993. Again, another order executed by Colonel Blaskic, and it goes to all brigades, all commanders of independent units, the Vitezovi, Trvkto, the 4th Military Police Battalion and others and reads as follows: "The rising number of soldiers deserting their positions and defence lines has resulted in the loss of defended facilities and the entire defence lines. In order to prevent such occurrences, I hereby issue the following: 1. Undertake the following disciplinary measures against any soldier and their immediate commander who desert defence lines. A) execution of the unit/soldier; B) unit commanders will be declared traitors of the nation and given the most severe sentence of death by firing squad in front of the unit. 2. All units and soldiers will be notified of this order. 3. This order will come into force immediately, and commanders of brigades and independent units will be responsible to me for its execution." My question for you, Brigadier, as the Chief of Staff and as a man who was close to Colonel Blaskic: Where did Blaskic find the power to order that soldiers and commanders be executed if they desert the lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the source for issuing authorisations of this kind, but I do recall the contents of this order. I recall the time it was issued, and as far as I know, it was issued on the basis of a command by the head of the main staff. And the object was to frighten the soldiers, that is, to make them become serious in their duties and in connection to their combat assignments. Because we see that the date is the 11th of October 1993, when the HVO and the units in Central Bosnia and in all the enclaves were at their last, on their last strengths. It was, therefore, to frighten the soldiers, because in point 2 it says all units and soldiers should be informed of this order; so this kind of order issued, of course, it was never implemented and the order was never executed over anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first off, on this order, Brigadier, there is no reference on this order that such an order was given by the HVO main staff in Mostar; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, as far as I recall, this document was written on the basis of that. I remember the contents of the document and I remember the object, why it was written and under what circumstances it was written, and I have explained that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Brigadier, death by firing squad is, of course, the most severe form of penalty that anybody could suffer from; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and in this case, this could never be ordered by General Blaskic, and that is why this particular order, according to its contents, was never put into practice. Nobody was sentenced to death by a firing squad. So, the aim was to make the soldiers more serious and frighten them. And in point 2 it says inform all units and soldiers of this order, so the commanders were given instructions to read out the text to the soldiers so the soldiers would come to realise just how serious the situation was. You can see from the order, the shock terms used by General Blaskic, when he talked about stopping the destruction of houses and the burning of houses and civilians, so he used energetically and most seriously, and all the terms used in that kind of terminology for that particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, Brigadier, that this particular order, based on the received stamp from Emil Heran, the head of the brigade commander of the Bobovac Brigade was received in Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kara (phoen).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this document, the commander of the brigade in Vares. And this can be seen from the upper right-hand corner. So this document was written, was copied out as he received it from the commander at Operative Zone, and you can see that from the document itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the first order that you have, Exhibit 456/74, which is the other order to execute; was that also based on an order from headquarters? We're talking about the 24th of October, 1992 order, when Mensud Alic was ordered to be arrested, and if he resisted, execute him. So you'll notice it has no reference point back to anything from HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For this particular document, number 456/74, I did not know about the document, the text itself speaks of the circumstances, and how to act in those circumstances. I don't know the source of this information, that is, from whence the information came, but Mr. Mensud Alic had started out towards Travnik. But, as far as I know, this did not happen, either. So, I do not know that this happened, that is, that Mr. Mensud turned up, or that he was arrested or that he was killed. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me shift gears, Brigadier, and talk about punishment given to special purpose units, PPN units. On page 12.189, the question by Mr. Nobilo was as follows: "Tell the Court, could Colonel Blaskic and the disciplinary court and the prosecutor's office, could it punish members of the PPN units?" And your answer was: "No, we do not have the necessary competence for this." Do you recall that statement and do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that statement and I recall the answer. And that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just emphasise that the units which were not within the composition of the Operative Zone, that is to say, those units who were under operative command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the individual by the name of Zuti was, ran a PPN unit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Zuti units, the yellow units, was within the composition of the Frankopan Brigade, so it was not a unit organisationally linked directly to the Defence Ministry or any other institution. It was a unit which, that is to say, a group of 30 individuals who proclaimed themselves to be special purpose units, and they acted within the frameworks of the Frankopan Brigade, just as a company or platoon within the framework of the brigade. The special purpose units, which were not organisationally linked to the commander of the Operative Zone, was the military police and the Vitezovi, the Knights; whereas, all the other special purpose units were in the composition of the brigades. And they endeavoured, that is to say, they were made up of specially trained individuals. There were 30 soldiers, and they proclaimed themselves to be special purpose units, but they acted within the composition of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Brigadier, we're not going to go through the entire organisation of the brigade again. What is your question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you're telling us that there are some PPN units that Blaskic could have punished and some PPN units that he could not have punished; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, units, special purpose units within the frameworks of brigades could be punished by General Blaskic, but the other ones not within the composition of the Operative Zone could not have been punished, and these are the Vitezovi, The Knights, and the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about Exhibits 237 and 239. Those are Defence Exhibits 237 and 239, and also Defence Exhibit 213. Brigadier, the first two exhibits, 237 and 239, are disciplinary orders, I'm sorry -- are disciplinary orders that were given by Colonel Blaskic against members of the Zuti PPN unit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from this order you can see what I stated a moment ago. And it says that in document number -- just one moment please, 239, on page 1, it states that Borobon Zvenivic and the PPN Zuti, the yellows of the Frankopan Brigade, which means this special purpose unit was within the composition of the Frankopan Brigade. And that is what happened in Novi Travnik, there were others, they were called Grasshoppers there, or any other term. But from this document you can see precisely what I claimed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let me show you Defence Exhibit 213, which is the report that was issued by the military police after Zuti and his men broke one of their members out of the military prison in Kaonik. You talked about that report, and you talked about that being a significant event in Central Bosnia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was a significant event, first of all, because the members of, with PZO arms came to the command of the military police, so as to influence the outcome related to the detainees from their unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, as the chief of operations did Blaskic ever issue an order to arrest, to investigate, to detain or to otherwise discipline any member or Zuti or any member of his unit for this outrageous piece of conduct that you discussed during your direct testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes, an investigation was initiated. The outcome of it is not known, and the punishment, the sanctions proclaimed are not known. Had I, if I had the document, I would recall it, perhaps, as I do the event. But I do know that an investigation was initiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, you recall the event, but you don't recall the result of any investigation of this outrageous event; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the outcome of the investigation. I said that as far as investigations are concerned, I told you what I can say about it. If somebody conducted an investigation, in this case I imagine this should have been the security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let me ask you another question: So, you said there are PPN units that Zuti, that Blaskic could have disciplined, but other special purpose units, like the Vitezovi, that Blaskic could not discipline; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it become evident to Blaskic and to you and to other members in the HVO staff that members of the Vitezovi had committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally, I personally did not have any concrete facts or events proving that the Vitezovi unit had committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not. But if I didn't know, and I'm speaking in my own name, because had General Blaskic known I would have known, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, as far as you know, there were no facts in the possession of either Blaskic or you that the Vitezovi had committed any war crimes at all; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I am responsible for the Vitezovi unit as a whole. But whether an individual from Vitezovi, or a group of five or ten, or six people committed certain war crimes, that I cannot confirm. But, the unit, as such, whether it received orders from General Blaskic, and whether they did that, I don't know. Or rather I know they never got the order to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a mistranslation. The witness said that he is responsible, but he meant that he was responding, that he is replying to the question. And answering a question and answering to someone is a different thing. So, please let us clarify this with the witness. Is he answerable for the actions of the Vitezovi, or is he answering the question put to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What was the question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're moving down on the list, I'm not sure what the translation was. The folks in the translation booth translated what the witness said. If they want to ask in redirect to clarify it, I invite them to do so. The time is running out, I have questions I would like to get through before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could have a copy of that page of the transcript for, if the Court can provide that, we don't have a way to generate that immediately; otherwise it's lost, that's why Mr. Nobilo mentioned it, because if we don't mention it, it's lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, can we have a copy of that page?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, continue, you still have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, when was the first time that you and Blaskic and the other headquarters concluded that the 4th military police had committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it working now? Do you hear now, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never, in 1993, or today, was in the opportunity, or did I have at my disposal facts that would show that the military police had committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me ask you some questions. To your knowledge as chief of operations and as the deputy commander, did Blaskic ever arrest, punish, discipline, or dismiss any HVO commander or soldier for burning Muslim property, for destroying Muslim sacral objects, such as mosques, for killing Muslim civilians or non-combatants, for forcing Muslim civilians and prisoners of war to dig trenches, for using Muslims and prisoners of war as human shields, plundering and looting Muslim property, unlawfully detaining Muslim civilians or unlawfully detaining Muslim civilians at a headquarters which is likely to be armed by hostile fire; all of those things, do you know of Blaskic ever arresting, punishing, disciplining any commander or any subordinate for any of that stuff, at any time? And if you do, please tell the Judges about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but I do know the following: That for destroying the mosque in Kiseljak he issued orders to investigate this event; that he issued orders to prohibit most strictly the destruction of mosques, and unsoldierly conduct with civilians; and everything else, as far as actions towards civilians is concerned, and which is in contravention to the Geneva Conventions, I said General Blaskic, that he did have the name and surname of -- had General Blaskic had the name and surname of the person who had burned and looted, he would have prosecuted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm almost completed these are the last three questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, take the Kiseljak mosque. After that issue of the destruction of the Kiseljak mosque came to the attention of Blaskic, was anybody in the HVO prosecuted or disciplined for the destruction of the mosque in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the mosque in Kiseljak is concerned, the order that we saw here, I don't know whether it was introduced by the Defence or the Prosecution, it is evident that General Blaskic ordered the commander of the operative group, or rather the commander of the Brigade Ban Jelacic, to investigate and ascertain facts related to this event. The reasons for this are well-known to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I hate to interrupt, Mr. President, with the time constraints; the question is a yes or no. Did you, was anybody disciplined for the destruction of the Kiseljak mosque? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was by General Blaskic. Now, whether the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, according to the orders received from General Blaskic, did he get a name or surname and take action, that I don't know, but as far as I know, General Blaskic did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were serving as a deputy military prosecutor, was anybody disciplined in the HVO for any of the crimes that we talked about? Was anybody disciplined for any of these crimes directed against the Muslim population; the burning of property, the destroying of mosques, killing of Muslim civilians, et cetera? To your knowledge, was anybody disciplined in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For such events, as far as I know, no one was punished, and I already said why there were no names, but may I recall -- Mr. President, may I just tell you one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, I think that you have explained the reasons. You don't have to justify yourself. We're simply asking a question. The question was to know whether, in fact, there were or there were not -- there was or there wasn't any punishment. That's point of the question. Do you still have another question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is the last. You're forcing me to be like a football referee, because we're counting this down. I know there were technical interruptions but it's the last question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, the bottom line is; as far as you know, no HVO members are either prosecuted or disciplined by the military authorities for the crimes that we talked about, the burning of Muslim property, the destroying of Muslim sacred sites, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not a question, Mr. Kehoe. Ask your question. You're making a comment about the answer of the -- so you're going to finish with your comment or you're going to finish with the question? You were allowed one question, no comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, no one was ever disciplined and no one was ever prosecuted for any of these crimes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question was asked. Mr. Nobilo, do you have amenity you'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly what you said just now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that you have finished, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have finished, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is for the Defence and for the Prosecution: When the parties are limited in time, they must ask questions very directly and very concisely. Remember, Mr. Kehoe, we could have been more concise and more direct for several days already. All right. The cross-examination is now finished. You know that according to the Rules and Statutes the Defence counsel can now use the witness for re-examination. You spoke about how many -- how much time? Do you think that you're going to finish by 1.00, Mr. Nobilo? There's going to be a break, as we ordinarily have, around 11.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm afraid that according to my calculations, after more than two weeks of cross-examination the two hours or two and a half hours would be the minimum time I require, but I'm really going to act in haste, and I'm going to put a minimum of questions and we have no intention of keeping the Brigadier longer than necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to speak with my colleagues once again. We spoke a little bit together last night, but I would like to consult them again. Mr. Nobilo, Mr. Hayman, for your re-examination you have until 1.00, and then you will have 30 minutes when we begin again in the afternoon. That's 30 minutes between 2.30 and 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So it be, Mr. President, we respect your order, but we object, having placed us under an overall limit, which would properly incentivise the Defence to use its time wisely, to place specific time limits on our examination, particularly two and half or less than two and a half hours after two weeks of cross-examination, I think that is inconsistent with the framework that the Court established in terms of an overall time limit. If there is an overall time limit, this is the Defence's time, and if Mr. Nobilo needs two and a half hours or two hours and 45 minutes, we submit that hold us to our overall limit, but you should not place this type of additional limit on us, because it has no effect on the overall length of the trial. Unlike a limit on the Prosecutor's time, he was not using his time, he was using our time, as I understand the Court's ruling, during cross-examination. So we were not similarly situated with the Prosecutor, and there is not the same reason or justification to put a specific time limit on redirect. I think Mr. Nobilo has said he's going to move quickly and expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That may give you an answer. Let me remind you from the Rules and Statute, the Judges have a right to say at what point they consider that they have been sufficiently informed about all of the questions that were dealt with. That's the basic and legal point. In fact, we could go on and on speaking about the time that you've been given, and, Mr. Hayman, you could even be given, as part of the Defence time, another eight days for your re-examination, but we Judges, we consider that after three weeks of hearing this witness, it is now time to conclude, and that by giving you two or two and a half hours for re-examination is sufficient to allow you to clarify the questions that you want to ask, and which allow you to respond to some parts of the cross-examination. Let us not waste any more time now. Judge Riad says that you yourself are the one who said it was for two hours or two and a half hours. Let's not waste any more time. If you agree go, Mr. Nobilo, go right into your re-examination, understanding that it will be over at 3.00. Go ahead. Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So at this point in time we start, and I suggest that we place on the ELMO this document so that the numbers could be seen, please. Could I please approach the easel?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, the documents which you are giving us here are D406 and 408 and 404; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And 407 and 408, but it's not important to have all those documents now, but for orienting the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier Marin, the Presiding Judge, Mr. Jorda, also said -- noted that the numbers on the orders of General Blaskic were rising, jumping. I think that was the word used by the Judge. So could you explain to the Court how these numbers were formed by using, as an example, some of the documents we already introduced, D405, D404, D406, D407 and D408. So do you please explain to the Court how these numbers were established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the establishment of numbers in 1993, in the command of the operative zone, was defined by the very internal organisation of this command. The establishment of a number was done in the following way: I draw your attention to the following schematic. Number 01, number 01, that is a document, a document. That is to say, when a document is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. On the screen -- I don't see it on the screen. What is it, -- all right. I think we should see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is 406 now; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps the camera could zoom in on this number -- this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is to say, every document -- every document where General Blaskic's text -- name is at the end of the text, that means that his document, and the reference number is 01. Now, we do have on the monitor 406. That is this document, and also the same goes for number 405. That is to say that General Blaskic had the number 01. The head of staff had number 02. This is a document of the head of staff. This is document 407.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or document 408. It's all the same. Document 408 shows the same thing. Further on, the operational department that I headed had number 03, et cetera. That is to say, that in the command of the operative zone, the establishment of numbers, these reference numbers was conducted as follows: We had organisational units, and then we started from the commander, 01; the head of staff, 02; operative -- operations, 03; and then 04 was logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how many departments were there -- or, rather, how many numbers were there such as 01, 02, et cetera, that were used when setting up this reference number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Documents. To the best of my recollection, when these numbers were allocated in the command from 01 onwards, as far as I can remember, it went from 01 to 010. I could put this much more clearly if I had all the departments here now, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to shorten these proceedings, our time is short, and what did this reference number consist of, what numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reference number -- when this reference number is set up, it consisted of the following: That is to say, of the person who is the signatory of the document. If it is the commander, then it's his number. Then the month when the document was created -- the month when the document was created, and also the registered number -- I mean, that was registered in the book that was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He's pointing to something and the translation comes five, or six or ten seconds later. The Judges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Hayman is objecting to his own witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, but we are under pressure, under time pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have to slow down, Mr. President. This is very important, very complicated, very detailed, and it may take half an hour to explain but it's very important, and I'm just trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ask your witness, Mr. Hayman. Mr. Hayman, the problem of time relates very much to the way that the witness answers. I wanted to say that to you a while back. You are now suffering yourself in that the witness is unable to answer concisely. You can't do anything about it, nor can I, and we are wasting a lot of time. Brigadier, try to be clear and concise when you give your answers. We can ask this from an important military official. It can't be asked of all witnesses, but we can ask you. Each time you're asked a question, you go into very long comments, and this is why we have spent three weeks. Try to answer -- this is not the Prosecution but the Defence asking the question. Try to answer clearly and concisely. Mr. Nobilo, ask your question again but ask it clearly, and think about the interpreters. And this is for my benefit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. I shall try to guide the witness with my questions so that we would shorten this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, you said that every department had its own designating number from 01 to 010?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that that is the first part of the reference number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the second part of the reference number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second part of the reference number is the month when the document was created.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is the third part of the reference number established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third part of the reference number is established on the basis of the order in which documents arrive in the General Services Unit. So, for example, if there were 10 documents registered before a new document arrives, then the next document that arrives will be number 11, the document after that will be 12, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that in the general office you had one book of registry and one series of numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, and you can see this from this schematic on the establishment of a reference number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, for example, that when Colonel Blaskic, in document 405, is number 271, and after that you take up number -- the next numbers, and all the members of the operations department of Central Bosnia go in the same order, and then when Colonel Blaskic writes his next document, then there is a difference from 271 to 366 in the same month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That is what it means. That is what I explained before you put your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the reason why one person, regardless of whether it is Colonel Blaskic or you as the barer of number 03, have such different serial numbers within the same day and the same week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the main difference involved. And the difference between numbers is affected by the number of the documents that was created that day in the command, whether it was in logistics in the command, in the commander's office. So the sum of all these documents that were created in that day is equal to the number of documents that were registered that day. The registration of every document went in a certain order. If my document was created at 12.00, it was registered as being created at 12.00. If I made a document at 3.00 and if somebody else used reference numbers in the meantime, then perhaps it will be a difference of 3, 5 or 10 numbers. That is the kind of system we had of reference numbers in the command of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell us, to the best your recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell us, to the best of your recollection, when did you introduce this system of numbers and when did you move on to a different system of numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this system of numbers, this one here, as far as I remember, we introduced in mid December 1992, or the end of December 1992. I cannot recall the exact date. And this was internal within the command of the operative zone. When we got, from the Ministry of Defence, concrete instructions with numbers, then in the command of the operative zone and in the subordinate units that were within the command of the operative zone, we gave this assignment and we acted according to the instructions of the Ministry of Defence. To the best of my recollection, such a document did not arrive from the Ministry until the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, what we see here on this paper, who wrote this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made this schematic on the basis of the documents that were introduced by the Defence and the Prosecution, because these documents were numbered this document, this document, this document, so that on every copy that has one one could see how this number was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I kindly ask the registrar to tender this -- to register this, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Give it a number, a very simple number. What will the number be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D411.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's move to another area. At the beginning of the cross-examination you answered the Prosecutor's questions as to the numbers of the commands in the operative zone, and you introduced a document which stated that the operative zone and the command of the operative zone should have 105 individuals. The Defence showed you a document dated August 1993, as opposed to the first document which was 1992, which stated that the command should have 60 people. Could you tell the Trial Chamber -- please, now, you are working in the Federal army, you are head of the main staff of what is the equivalent of the corps for the operative zone. Tell the Court, please, in peacetime, that is to say not in wartime, effectively speaking, how many people work in the command in the Croatian component of the army of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the command of the -- and the staff today in peacetime, we have about 109, 110 people working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In peacetime, how many soldiers do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In peacetime, that is to say today, the first guard has about -- corps has about 10,500 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if there were to be a war, how many would you be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In wartime, that is to say wartime formations, the command of the first guard formation would have -- the corps would have 220,000 (sic) people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 16th of April the war broke out with the Muslims, and up to the first cease-fire of the 20th of April, that is to say in the four days of the most intensive fighting, how many of you were in the command of the Central Bosnia operative zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the days you mentioned, that is to say, from the 16th up to the cease-fire, in the command of the operative zone there were seven people working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There has been a mistake. It says that the corps has 220,000 people. That was an error. In the command of the corps in wartime the figure was 220 individuals. So there has been a misinterpretation, it was not 220,000 but 220. I'm going to ask you again, Brigadier, in case of war, in your corps, which is the equivalent for the operative zone, how many members would the staff have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There should be 220, 220 workers, 220 members of the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another area. We have been speaking at length about the educational and training structure, and you maintained that in the operative zone of Central Bosnia there were only three officers who had military academy training and experience in command posts, officers' posts, from the JNA. The Prosecutor showed you a series of names of individuals who were reservists, reserve officers, and who, during their military service, for six months attended a school for reserve officers. Do you still maintain that you did not have educated officers for the types of assignments and professional tasks in the operative zone of Central Bosnia in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I maintain that now, as well, and I note that in the brigades and in the command of the operative zone, that is to say of all the officers who were on duty there, nobody was capacitated to perform tasks that were entrusted to him at that time. And me too, as the commander of the operative department, was not trained to perform the assignments I was given because I had not been to the corresponding schools to perform those assignments, but the situation was such and I performed my duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell the Trial Chamber, please, when somebody goes to school for -- a reserve officer school for six months, which the JNA organised during military service, what rank would he receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After emerging from this particular school for non-commissioned officers, the rank would be First Lieutenant. When he goes back to his civilian duties and he has his wartime assignments, in his years of service, that is while he is a reservist, unless he performs professional duties he could reach the rank of Captain First Class. That is to say, he could perform the duty after commander of a company and have command over 110 to 120 individuals -- soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, in the command of the operative zone, did anybody -- was anybody capacitated to perform the functions command of the main staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the command of the operative zone, of all of us who were there at the time, nobody had been trained to perform the functions he was, in fact, performing, and neither was General Blaskic. Why? Because General Blaskic was trained and capacitated for a company commander. He had the rank of Captain First Class, but he had not graduated from any command school or main staff school, and he was performing functions of a two star general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, at least on paper, at one point you had 12 brigades, as much as 12 brigades. Now, tell the Court, to command a brigade in every conventional type of army, what rank must you hold and what kind of experience must you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to command a brigade in an organised army, you have to be a Colonel and have completed a school for commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 12 commanders of the brigade, did any one of them have such schooling? Had he completed -- graduated from a school of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of our brigade commanders had graduated from any school of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had 12 brigades, and on an average, each brigade had, let us say, three battalions, which makes a total of 36 battalions. So tell the Court, please, the commanders of the 36 battalions, did you have a single man commanding one of the 36 battalions having the prescribed educational level and training to command a battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not, because an officer, if he were to have the prescribed educational levels to perform battalion commander, would have to have the rank of major, he would have had to have completed military academy, and have completed a course in command, and in our battalions we did not have a single individual of that type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we had 36 battalions and each battalion had, let us say, three to four companies, without going into mathematical calculation, we are talking about 100 commanders of the companies, as you had reserve officers who were capacitated to command companies, can you then tell us whether at the level of companies you had trained officers who were able to command companies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have trained and capacitated commanders of companies. Why not? Because the officers who had been equipped and trained to command a company, had completed school, that they were at posts of the commanders of battalions and brigades in the commands of brigades, and in the commands of the operative zone. So that the commanders of the companies and platoons, in practical terms, were people without any kind of military training. That is to say, they were individuals who were chosen by the members of the units to be commanded by them in their villages and in the places where these units were set up and organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Tihomir Blaskic, the accused, had the rank of First Class Captain and had been trained to command a company. How many men does a company have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A company has between 100 to 120 men, depending on the kind of company it is. One hundred to one hundred and twenty soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, which rank and how many years of experience would a commander have to have of an operative zone or corps, whichever you like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to our organisation so far, and the first guard corps, which is based on NATO standards, the commander of an operative zone or commander of a corps would have to be a two star general, and he would have had to have completed his military academy or military school, staff schools, war schools, command schools, and at least 15 to 20 years of active service in the army with, of course, very good results in his work, and tried and tested capabilities of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you document 476, which represented the structure of the fourth corps of the Yugoslav People's Army. Tell the Court, please, having looked at the document and studied it, what were you able to ascertain? How many officers and what level was envisaged for the command of the corps of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having analysed the structure of the commanding officers of the 4th Corps offered by the Prosecutor, I ascertained the following: In that particular corps there should have been one officer with rank of General, 62 higher ranking officers, that is to say Majors or Colonels, 25 First Class Captains, and if we add this together, 91 officers in the command of a corps of the rank shown to us and in the documents shown to us by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had seven during the April war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me move on to another area now, and I would have to prepare some documents for that. So perhaps we could take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters also need a break. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sorry for the delay. I am adjusting, but the clocks are not all the same in the Tribunal. You're not going to have 30 minutes, but 40 minutes this afternoon, Mr. Nobilo, so you can be reassured. But that does not apply to the Prosecution, or did not apply to the Prosecution this morning. Mr. Nobilo, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to a new area. The Prosecutor showed you documents from which it emerged that in the Operative Zone you were commanded to determine in which units there were members of the Croatian army, the HV; and you said that you received a command from the main staff and that you further sent it further down the line. Tell the Court, please, what was the reason for you to issue a command to the brigades to determine who belonged, and whether in your area there were members of the Croatian army, although you knew there were no such members? Why did you issue this order? What was the reason for issuing an order under these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the order by General Blaskic, the commander of the Operative Zone, concerning data on whether there were officers of the Croatian army in our brigades was written and came into being on the basis of an order from the head of the main staff. It was on the basis of that order that we had to write our own order, in turn, and in the text, and according to its contents, it is exactly the same as the commander of the main staff. Had the commander of the main staff sent a questionnaire as to whether we had formations linked to this, then we could answer on the basis of our facts and figures; but the order was given, so it had to be dispatched to the commands of subordinate units, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, this order, its preamble does not refer to the commander of the chief of the main staff, which you issued in the Operative Zone; how do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, why there is no preamble, that is to say, the preamble on the title of the document, on the basis of which our order was written, as I know the man who wrote it, he does not have military training at all, and I think that is one of the main reasons that is not stated here, because he wrote this order in a non-professional way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now take a look, please, at two documents, one of them is 406, P406/26, and the other is 406/27, and another document, 406, was issued by Tihomir Blaskic and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and the second document, 406/27, was issued by Zeljko Siljeg, the commander of the Operative Zone of north-western Herzegovina. And to make matters short, I am going to read Blaskic's order, and what is required. With each of my sentences, you can read what Siljeg asked for. And it is an order from the Operative Zone dated the 5th of October, 1992, and the order of the Operative Zone for north-western Herzegovina of the 6th of October. So, I'm going to read your Operative Zone Central Bosnia order. The first thing you asked for is the first name, the father's name and the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Now, read out exactly what Zeljko Siljeg asked for in the 2nd Operative Zone a day later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command to the north-western Herzegovina Brigades with its headquarters in Tomislavgrad, and he is asking of its units the first name, father's name and last name, he is asking for that, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'm reading the second line of the order: The date of birth, the place and municipality of birth, that is what Blaskic is calling for; and he is calling for the same; the date, place and municipality of birth. And now I'm reading the third line of Blaskic's order, which is the personal number, rank and a number of the promotion of the decree. What is Siljeg asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same, the JNB, the personal identification number, and the rank and promotion order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. President, everything else is identical, too, so this will save us reading the document in full. What do you deduce from the fact that in two orders in two Operative Zones the same wording, the same text is used, the same commas, if you will, and in fact, it is absolutely identical; what can you conclude from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this I conclude that this order, in the command of the Operative Zone, was written on the basis of the order from the commander of the main staff, which sent his order to all the Operative Zones, and here we have an example of the Operative Zone for north-western Herzegovina. According to the date of the document, you can see these two documents were written on the basis of the command from the commander of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, may I have documents 406, P407? These are also two orders issued by Blaskic and Zeljko Siljeg, that is to say, commanders of two Operative Zones, both orders are dated the 12th of April, 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read a text from Blaskic's order, the first sentence, point 1, and then you read point 1 from Siljeg. So, Blaskic says, "Submit a list of all officers of--

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, what exhibit is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 406/54 and 406/55, Prosecutor's Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. You didn't mention those, or they didn't come across in the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, we have two orders which speak of establishing a list of Croatian officers into the HVO. I'm reading point 1 of Blaskic's order from the 12th of April, 1993. "Submit a list of all officers of the Croatian army in your units and commands." Please read point 1 of the order issued by Zeljko Siljeg from Operative Zone Central Bosnia dated the same date, that is to say, the 12th of April 1993, north-west Herzegovina that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Submit the list of all Croatian army officers present in your units and headquarters."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am reading the second point of the Tihomir Blaskic's order. "In addition to the name, give the father's name, last name, number of the order with which he was sent to the HVO, rank and number of transfer decree," and now there is something illegible. We cannot see quite clearly because it is illegible. Could you please read these few words from the order of Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rank and transfer --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, from the very beginning, read point 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the order of the Operative Zone of north-west Herzegovina it says: "In addition to name, father's name and last name, submit the orders which authorised his referral to the HVO, rank and number of decree of promotion, (reserve and career), the duty he is currently carrying out in your army and the duties he has carried out so far."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell us, these two texts, are they literally identical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these two texts are absolutely identical, and they were created on the basis of the order of the head of the main staff, which is clear from the preamble of the command issued by the commander of north-west Herzegovina, and which is also obvious from the date that was created when this was created in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, and of north-west Herzegovina respectively, and that is the 12th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the order from the Operative Zone of north-west Herzegovina has a preamble, and it is shown on which basis this order is issued, and the order from Central Bosnia does not have a preamble. Could you read the preamble of the order from north-west Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order issued by the main staff of the HZ H-B number 01-618/83 of the 12th of April, 1993, and with the purpose of completing the records and defining the status of Croatian army officers in the HVO, I issue the following order."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So, do you still maintain that you issued orders on checking whether there are members of the Croatian army in your Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exclusively on the basis of the orders issued by the higher command, yes, I maintain that assertion, and I maintain the assertion that in the command and the units of the operative command of Central Bosnia there were no officers of the Croatian army or soldiers of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to a new area. I'm asking for document 406/56, Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/56. Brigadier, if you remember the Prosecutor showed you this document. This is a letter of the HVO of the Travnik municipality, that is to say, the civilian structures of the Travnik municipality sent to the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman. I'm going to read out to you a quotation which I believe is relevant, and then I'm going to put a few questions to you. The quotation in the original is on page 2 in the last section, where it says: "Dear Mr. President," in the middle of this paragraph, "It would be helpful to us if, from the Republic of Croatia, which is being used as a country of transit, it would be very helpful if you would prevent the entry of foreign nationals which come from Islamic countries and who are fighting here in the ranks of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and who are fighting against everything that is Croatian and Christian here." And then the next section. "It would be very helpful if you would, once again, instruct your assistants to send to this area senior officers of the Croatian army headed by General Praljak to consolidate our units in the Lasva Valley." Brigadier, what is your comment, in view of the fact that the municipality of Travnik, that is to say, a civilian structure, is writing to the president of a different state? Is this something that should be customary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is obvious from this letter that the municipal authorities are directly addressing the president of a state, which is to say that they are behaving as a state, as one state. About these problems, they should be writing to the central authorities of Herceg-Bosna, or of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, they don't do that. They are directly addressing the president of a state, and they are avoiding all other institutions, side stepping them. And this most evidently shows how municipal authorities behaved, and this is only one example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Another question. The civilian structures of one municipality ask for military officers which should come to the Lasva Valley and consolidate the defence; what does that say to you, and what is your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This directly speaks of the following: That municipal authorities have an influence over military affairs, and that they directly wish to influence personnel policies in the army. But it also shows another thing, which I kept highlighting here, and that is that the municipal authorities are concluding that there aren't any trained officers, that is to say, officers who are trained for the posts that they hold, and that they are trying to find them in this way, in another state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, please tell the Court, General Praljak, who was then a general in the Croatian army, with his officers, had he come to the Lasva Valley, what would that have meant? Who would have commanded the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had General Praljak, as requested by the municipal authorities, come to the command of the Operative Zone, it is logical that, due to his rank, he would have been commanding the Operative Zone, and the officers who would have come with him would have performed certain duties instead of us who were there in the command of the Operative Zone. However, according to this letter, according to the request made by this letter, these officers never came. General Praljak never came to command the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This letter was written on the 12th of April, 1993. On the 16th of April, 1993, four days later, war broke out. In those four days, did anyone come from the Croatian army? You said that Praljak didn't come, but did anyone come from the Croatian army before you were fully surrounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one came from the Croatian army in this period of time to the command of the Operative Zone, or to the area covered by the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We shall refer very briefly to the next area. Why, from the 16th of April 1993, when the war with the Muslims broke out, and until the 20th of April 1993 when some kind of a cease-fire was carried out and Blaskic went to Zenica for talks, why didn't anyone from the command of the Operative Zone go to the ground within those four days to check the units and to report directly to Blaskic as to what he saw at the combat positions and what he saw in the villages of the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in my statement, when I was questioned by the Defence, I said that that morning when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 16th of April, carried out attack against HVO units in the Lasva Valley in the command, there were only 7 of us there, and I was the only one involved in operations. And taking into account these numbers, it was impossible to do anything outside the command itself, and there wasn't anyone who could go to see the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next point. We spoke a lot about the principle of voluntariness. The Prosecutor showed you many documents from which it stems that Blaskic, on several occasions, in April, 1992, in July, in September, in October and in November, 1992, and also in February, 1993, asked for this voluntariness to be abolished. Please tell this Court, Brigadier, what conclusion do you draw from the fact that Blaskic has to repeat an average of every other month this kind of order? And if not, why did he not manage to do away with the principle of voluntariness in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true these orders were issued. Why were they issued? They were issued because on the ground they were not being carried out completely at all. In my judgement, and on the basis of what I know about the organisational set up of the army at that time in the area of the Lasva River Valley, or in the Operative Zone, is as follows: At that time units were established on a voluntary basis, that is to say, in the villages, and the commanders were elected, too. And practically this could not have been broken up. That is to say, people did not want this to be broken up. So, the units established in villages, and volunteers were defending their homes directly, and they have their own logic of behaviour which deviate from military principles and logic. I remember when I came to these units on various occasions, they would tell me, "we don't need any kind of commander, we are defending our own village and we know what we're going to do," that is exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell the Court, nevertheless, generally speaking, was this principle of voluntariness broken up somehow? If so, when, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, when I analysed the situation during 1993, I may state that October, November, December, 1993, that the logic, according to which people acted, that is to say, that the principle of voluntariness had to be there was a bit changed. Why? We came to a different, into a different situation, and people realised that if they were not guided by military logic we would all go down the drain, or rather we could not defend ourselves, and that practically we would be expelled or that the HVO units would be defeated by the BH army. So, this is just a small step forward when people realised there was no way out of a given situation, and that after ten months or so they realised military logic is the kind of logic that one has to pursue both in a unit and in war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, now we move on to a different subject. We are not going to offer any documents, in order to speed up matters, but for the purpose of the transcript, I wish to mention Prosecutor's Exhibit 481. The Prosecutor showed you this, and it says that special purpose units in the military police should recruit young men with such and such characteristics. So, one could derive from that document that some kind of selection was being carried out in the military police. And according to the Prosecutor's intention, this is in opposition to what you had been saying, that that is there was no selection made for the military police. Can you explain this to the Court? And do you still maintain your original assertion? If so, why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, I maintain my assertion, that is, that for the military police, for the military police, there was no selection except for the establishment of special purposes units within the military police. I don't know exactly, I think this unit had a total of 15 men, and the entire military police that went throughout the central, the zone of Central Bosnia had a total of 400 men; so for this entire military police there were no defined standards. Young men who wanted to go to the military police were recruited as volunteers, just as they entered other units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, in a telegraphic fashion, we move on to a different subject area, and I'm asking you directly. In January, or at any other time after that, did Tihomir Blaskic had have a different office in his capacity as commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia in Kiseljak? Did he have an office in Kiseljak outside of the Hotel Vitez or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the war General Blaskic did not have a different office or a different command post, except for the Vitez Hotel. So, he did not have it in the region of Kiseljak, either. I said that during the January conflicts General Blaskic just accidentally happened to be in the area of Kiseljak, and that as he was acting as commander, he used the seal of the commander of the brigade and he used the offices and the communications that this brigade had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on further. When we talked about training, we also talked about barracks, and the Prosecutor asked you in detail about all the different barracks, and you said that all barracks under HVO control were essentially warehouses, except the one in Kiseljak and in Travnik. So, please tell the Court, out of total of 8.400 men that you had under arms, how many soldiers were accommodated in barracks during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In these two barracks that you mentioned, which were built functionally for putting up an army, in that period of time for which you are asking me, to the best of my recollection, there was never more than 100 soldiers; however, there is one specific characteristic involved, as far as the Travnik barracks are concerned. After the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina took away the barracks from the former JNA, the two armies moved in there together, the HVO and the BH army, and the HVO soldiers were there until refugees came to the area of Travnik from places where the army of Republika Srpska had expelled the Muslim Bosniak population and the Croatian population. These are the following locations. Kljuc, Petrovac, Bosanska Krupa, Banja Luka, that is to say the area of north-west Bosnia. After that, in Travnik, in the Travnik barracks, there weren't any members of the HVO left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that after that, only Kiseljak had some soldiers in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We spoke of the shortages of the -- the shortcomings of the HVO organisation and the distinction between an armed people and the regular army of a State, and in that context you spoke about training, and on that basis, for two afternoons or for an entire day the Prosecutor asked you a series of questions. So tell the Court, are you denying that HVO soldiers had some kind of training in terms of using weapons, small arms or whatever? Was that the shortcoming? That was what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I meant in my testimony. I did not deny that there was training of individuals. However, in the structure of training as an activity which is carried out within the army, there is training of an individual, of a soldier, there is training of a unit, of a unit as a whole, and there is training of the command. In the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, we did not have conditions or the right people who could carry out the training of a platoon, of a battalion or brigade, that is to say up to 2.000 people, and in carrying out defence or attack activities, we did not have this kind of training. Also, we did not have training of the command of the brigade of a battalion, of the command of the Operative Zone, in terms of their duties that they're supposed to carry out during the war. That is to say either in defence or an attack, how all of this should function, how orders should be issued, how organisations should be set up, how reporting and control should be set up, and how tactically one should act in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please speak a bit slower, because I imagine this is very hard on the Prosecutor. We haven't got much time left, but it is important to make what we are saying understandable. You said that you did not have training of units from the command cadre. What about the units -- what about tactical training? Did that mean training of the units? And what does tactical unit training mean, and what was done in terms of reporting and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were no training of the units, and this kind of training is tactical training, that is how to use the unit, how to command and issue orders to the unit, how to exchange information, how to report, how to coordinate activities and how to control everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell us, please, was it simple for the functioning of the line of command, chain of command, was it essential for a soldier to be able to shoot properly or to throw a bomb properly, or was it essential to have tactical training of units and commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was important? Well, for the system of command, for the command process itself, it was important how and in what way the commander and the commanding officers were functioning, whether they were capacitated to control, to issue commands, to report and to organise all the business that was under his command and assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, tactical training. I've seen it many times in films, and fighting in built-up areas and populated areas. Now, what problems there are related to control on the part of the commander, and reporting of his -- reporting by subordinates to their commanding officers at the place where the fighting is taking place, and how do we promote the functioning of units in settlements in populated areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fighting in populated and built-up areas, in the theory and tactics that we applied and that I studied, the theory of tactics studied in the former Yugoslav People's Army, this is treated as being the most sophisticated and complicated type of fighting because it is in a populated area, which makes commanding difficult, it makes control difficult, and, therefore, it makes the overall functioning of the system of command more difficult. Therefore, under situations of this kind, the commander commanding a unit in a populated area is faced with a very difficult situation in controlling the state of affairs and the developments in the battlefield and in the populated area where the fighting is taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the units to become trained to fight in populated areas, what is undertaken in armies, and were you able to undertake this kind of training in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For us to train the unit and to capacitate the commander to be able to command in a populated area, what had to be done was to tactically train the units and the commander in performing their duties, and we did not implement this kind of training in the course of 1993 and 1994, and even today we haven't reached the level of capacitation that we can in peacetime implement this kind of training, because it is a highly complex form of training which requires high quality instructors and professionally trained officers specifically for that kind of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Brigadier, am I right in saying that I personally looked at special purpose units of the Croatian police which were using stage sets, as in theatres, to train themselves for fighting in a populated area? Is this a customary way of training units for fighting in populated areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of the ways, and it does look like a stage set, as you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on. The Prosecutor showed you Prosecution Exhibit 484, which represents the plan and programme for training of the new people to the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna. Tell us, please, when you trained people who had no training and came to you without any experience, that is to say, very young men, and up to what level of tactical training did you train these novices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, for me to be better understood, let me say what a novice is. A novice is a young man who has -- who is 18 years of age and who has had no military training up to that age. The training of such young men in the Lasva River Valley was organised in September, 1993, and on the basis of the plan and programme which was offered by the Prosecutor here. Due to the state of war that existed and the fact that we did not have adequate programs and training facilities, we realised this in an abridged form, and the highest level of tactical training with young men of that particular age, and within the frameworks of that kind of training was to train them up to the level of a platoon. That is to say, 30 soldiers, and how they are to be behave in a given situation, whether they are dealing with a forest area in the mountains or in plains. So different types of combat activity, defence activities, offensive activities and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May we proceed. The Prosecutor asked you about snipers and their weapons. Could you please tell the Court, did you have sniper units, that is to say, were there individuals who had something that could be termed a sniper or a weapon like a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
