There are the Judges questions, of course, that will be asked. Brigadier, you cannot yet leave because we have questions to ask, we're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, we are almost at the end of this long testimony. I will give the floor to my colleagues so that they can ask the questions which they feel are appropriate. Let me begin with Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, General, Brigadier Marin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you might cast some light, or some bit more light on some of your conclusions, some of which seem equivocal to me, specifically as regards to your diagnosis of the events to which you were privileged witness. The first conclusion, which seems a bit equivocal to me, related to the origins of the war in Central Bosnia between the Croats and the Muslims. I noted that you said that the Muslims had quickly abandoned the ground to the Serbs, they didn't know how to defend themselves, and the Serbs were able to gain territory, which would imply that they were weak, they were much weaker than the Serbs, that in fact they were really conquered. And yet, they opened up another front and attacked the Croats. What strategy could that serve, that is, to have a weak army opening up another front? Could you explain to me what strategy that could be? All the more so, all the more so, since you indicated in one of the documents that General Blaskic declared that the Muslims did not want the war against the Croats, that is document, I believe, 276, how can you reconcile those two observations which are more or less irreconcilable, that is, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, when I spoke about the fact that the army of the Republika Srpska had very quickly, in an easy way, expelled the Bosniak Muslims, and that portion of the Croats who lived in the municipality that I'm not going to mention, when I spoke of the time of the very beginnings of the aggression, in fact, of the army of the Republika Srpska on Bosnia-Herzegovina, in that part of my testimony I mentioned the following municipalities: I mentioned the municipalities of western Bosnia, that is to say, Kljuc, Petrovac, Prijedor, Banja Luka, Skender Vakuf, Donji Vakuf, Bosanska Krupa, and several other places, which are in that area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is in these places, Mr. President, and Your Honours, that the Bosniak Muslims, according to the population census of 1991, they were a relative and somewhere an absolute majority. However, in those places the Croats were represented to a small amount, and the HVO was not organised in those places. Now, what does that mean? It means that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the political leadership of the Muslims and Bosniaks at the beginning of the aggression of the army of the Republika Srpska, helped by the Yugoslav People's Army in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wavered, they were not decisive and resolute in standing up to that aggression, and this assertion I illustrated by the facts and stated the destinies of the Bosniak Muslims in the municipalities I mentioned. However, on the other side we have a different development of events. That is to say, in places where the Croats were, perhaps, a relative majority in some places, or the same percentage as the Muslim Bosniaks, and where the HVO was organised, that is to say, where the HVO was organised, together with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there a resistance was made to the army of the Republika Srpska. We have a comparison there. For example, Donji Vakuf, where the Muslim Bosniaks were the majority, the army of the Republika Srpska was able to take control in one day. However, Jajce, if we look at it on the map, is in the interior where there are Croats and the HVO exists and where it is working jointly with the Territorial Defence at the time of the Bosnian army, Jajce defended itself right up to the end of November, that is to say, the end of October, 1992. So, my observation and conclusion referred to the successes of the army of the Republika Srpska compared to the municipalities where the Muslim Bosniak population was a majority. And at the time it was the beginning of the aggression of the army of the Republika Srpska on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in that context, Mr. President and Your Honours, I made my observation that one of the reasons for doubt and dissatisfaction on the part of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the measures taken by the political leadership, when talking about aggression and standing up to that aggression, was that wavering or indecision. I'm going to give you the example of the village of Ravno, which was first attacked, which was attached first in the aggression by the army of the Republika Srpska on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is a village with a large percentage, or perhaps 100 per cent Croat population; I remember, for example, the news on television or reports when the head of the Bosniak Muslims, who was a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the day, and was the presiding individual, said after that aggression, and after the fact that the village was completely burned to the ground and the people expelled, that it was not a war -- I will try and remember the statement -- he said "it's not our war." So in that context, Mr. President, I made the conclusions that I made and the statements that I made. And would you remind me, you had another part of the question, so as to give you a detailed answer? Will you repeat the second part of your question, please? Yes, I remember, the second part of your question referred to whether the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the state that existed, can open a second front towards the HVO. Yes, those are the facts, and that is the truth. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina openly attacked the HVO in January, and that was the year of 1993. The conflicts I mentioned occurred in March 1992. So, that is a year when certain movements had been made with regard to equipment organisation, system, and so on. I said that through the promotion activities in Central Bosnia, there were rumours, there was stories that certain extremists, which existed both in the ranks of the BH army and the HVO, and I'm speaking principally of the BH army, said we do not have enough forces to fight against the Serbs, but we have enough forces to fight against the Croats. And furthermore, the second reason why an open attack occurred on the BH units, in the HVO units in Central Bosnia, was that in Central Bosnia there was a concentration of the military industry, that is to say, in Konjic we had the production of ammunition, in Vitez we had an explosives factory, in Novi Travnik there was an ammunition factory, again, for guns, and in Travnik footwear and clothing was produced for purposes of the army. So, with this kind of goal in mind, and to master this territory, the BH army would gain all the prerequisites to be able to arm itself and re-equip itself and independently to produce everything it needed, equipment and armaments for waging a war. Second, the territory of Central Bosnia, and particularly the Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez and Novi Travnik municipalities, with their geographic distribution, are at key points on roads in Central Bosnia, communication lines. And I said that all wars in Bosnia-Herzegovina were, to all practical purposes, all the armies waging war in Bosnia-Herzegovina waged them for the communication lines. Those in control of the communication lines would be the winners of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. I would like to ask you to give us a shorter answer, that way we can finish this afternoon. When we hear you, it seems that the sudden defeat of the Muslims, at Donji Vakuf in particular, in one day, provoked discontent among the Croats, vis-à-vis the Croats who withdrew quickly. Can one say that that discontent provoked a certain type of aggression on the part of the Croats against the Muslims, in order to teach them a lesson? To teach them how to act? As you can say, give them a good spanking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not maintain that, I did not think that, and that was not how things stood. It was not to teach them a lesson, to teach anyone a lesson, in fact. But, it was, quite simply, that the Croats were not able to understand that the Muslim Bosniaks, at the start, immediately at the beginning, did not firmly stand up in defence of the places that I mentioned. Because there had, there did not have any different conditions in Zenica, in connection to Bosanska, Petrovac, because the population ratio was that the units could have been organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another clarification I would like to ask for, which has to do with the role of General Blaskic vis-à-vis orders. General Blaskic issued many orders to protect civilians. For example, I have documents here, D480, I'm not going to cite them all, but he gave the orders to protect civilians. He even gave orders for fighting. Frequently they were orders that I saw in the transcript, when I wasn't there, I'm not sure that it was 456, I believe, in which he was addressing himself to Vitezovi and to the military police. In an army worthy of its name, I suppose that one gives orders that can be carried out; which means that even the Vitezovi, that is the military police, were subordinate to General Blaskic and received orders from him, and that he could give orders to protect civilians. At the same time you said that sometimes the -- here I am saying one word -- that they were really bluff, because they could not be carried out, such as the orders to convict, condemn to death people, that these orders in fact were simply an illusion. Can you confirm the conclusion that the Prosecutor drew this morning, to which you did not answer; that is, that nobody was prosecuted for war crimes, and that the General Blaskic's orders were not obeyed, they were not followed by any serious steps taken in order to punish the guilty ones? I would add that as regards, for example, Ahmici, and this morning as well, I believe it was the Kiseljak mosque, when you were asked why there was no investigation or if there was an investigation; and you said "how can an investigation be carried out if you don't know the people who committed the atrocity?" But that's why the investigation is carried out, in order to find out who committed the acts. Why do you say, what reasons can you give for there having been no orders and there was no follow-up to the orders from General Blaskic which asked that the civilians be protected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Judge said, is it not logical that an order issued should be executed by the army? Yes, in an army which is organised, Your Honour, which has standards and codes of conduct that have been built up, in that kind of army orders are, of course, executed. The failure to execute orders in the HVO, but I don't want to say that no orders issued were implemented, but were not executed strictly, orders by the commander of the Operative Zone to the HVO units, is the result, and I have said that; that is the difference between the HVO as an armed force of Herceg-Bosna, what it should have been and what the HVO actually was. I said, Mr. President, that the organisation of the HVO began in villages where family relationships existed, and where you didn't want, where you had neighbourly relations and you didn't want to go against those relations. And so, at a lower level, because of this familiarity in the relationships that existed in the village, in practice, none of the tasks were implemented with regard to punishment. Second, the orders which were issued to protect civilians best testify to how much General Blaskic, as a professional soldier, invested efforts, under existing conditions, the conditions under which he lived and worked, so that he could, with his subordinates, create the, bring to bear that they should fight against crimes of this kind, and to prevent, in their units, appearances and phenomena of this kind. I said on several occasions all these criminal instances and conduct towards civilians, the burning of houses and so on, that many of these activities were done secretly in a covert fashion, because nobody wanted to do this and to have it known, widely known. And that is where the problem lies. Furthermore, the existence of informal groups, unofficial groups which had weapons at their disposal, you see the PPN, special purpose units in the brigades, for example 20 young men say they are a special brigade and give themselves the name of Grasshoppers, for example; and those 20 young men in the units, on the next day or two days later might leave the units. So, it was not, organisationally speaking, something that had been standardised and ordered. And it is for these reasons that the execution of orders was made more difficult. I said that as the war progressed, as people began to realise what war meant and what the dangers that war brought with it and what consequences it brought, already in 1993, on the eve of the Washington Accords, we had a higher degree of execution of the General's orders. The General was consistent and persistent in fighting against everything that was not in conformity with military ethics and logics and the Geneva Conventions and other agreements. Furthermore, when we come to the mosque in Kiseljak, he ordered the commander of the brigade to ascertain and investigate this incident and the state of affairs there. Furthermore, he ordered the commanders to send him the names and surnames of individuals who had burned houses, but he was never able to arrive at any name. Why not? Because the commander of the brigade could not arrive at a name himself. So the commander of the brigade did not refuse to execute that order, he was just not able to implement it, because he did not get the right information, that is to say, someone with a name and surname was the perpetrator of one of these incidents. So the key problem was that the HVO was badly organised, was in the process of being established and being born, and not a well organised army at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you tell me succinctly, if there were any people, and name them if you can, any people who were prosecuted for war crimes? I accept that one could not condemn to death, as we spoke about at great length yesterday, because that might have caused trouble in the army, and it might have had an effect on the General's popularity. But even theoretically were any prosecutions for war crimes carried out against certain individuals? And who were they? That's all. In general, as regards all the incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, there was no such prosecution, but investigations had been ordered. We saw what General Blaskic got when he ordered investigation of certain cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another question about which I would like some clarification. One has constantly said that the General was not able to appoint or dismiss commanders, that he needed the consent, or perhaps consultation with the local authorities. Were there any cases when communal or local authorities opposed the appointments or dismissals of General Blaskic on the ground, in fact, did he ever run into any opposition to what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when dismissals were concerned, we have the case of Fojnica, when appointments are concerned, General Blaskic, because he was aware of what the situation was, he knew what the situation was, what he could and could not carry out. I said that he was balancing between his powers and the actual situation on the ground. He was in a position to reconcile two opposites, on the one hand he had powers, and on the other hand he could not carry them out in practice. Mr. President, I will go a step further, as far as appointments are concerned. Even the municipal authorities could not impose a commander of a brigade if the army did not want it in the lower units. Also, the commander of a battalion could not be appointed if he were not accepted by the soldiers he was supposed to command. So, we would get down to village level, to company level, where you could not decree anyone, appoint anyone by decree. Not in a single case in Central Bosnia, in the Lasva Valley, General Blaskic or any commander could not appoint an officer, who was professionally trained, to appoint him to be a commander in a different village in a different unit. I mean, two people from a different village where this person did not live. For example, in the village of Krcevine, there could only be a commander from the village of Krcevine, no matter how many able men you had, or in the village of Jardol, or wherever, that was the reality and the state of affairs. Because if you would appoint a person who these people did not want, he could not work with these people. They would refuse to carry out every one of his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Does this also apply to dismissals? Could he dismiss somebody from a community and replace him by somebody else from the same community, in order to please that community? Or was even that difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not even carry that out. That is to say, that the person he wanted to appoint would have to be approved of by the people this person would command. So, if it was a lower level unit, a company or whatever, 30 people, 100 people, that is to say the entire structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He could not dismiss people, that's the question, he could not dismiss people. He could not take them out of service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not, he could not, although he did have the legal authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Last question. I have noted that you said in the hearing of 6 October that you could not assert whether officers or Croatian soldiers were participants in the HVO; and furthermore, yesterday or perhaps this morning, we spoke about a request, about a letter which was sent by the municipality on 12 April 1993 to the president of Croatia, or to General Praljak, it was the general of the Croatian army, asking that he send higher ranking officers in order to re-enforce the Lasva Valley units. The fact that municipalities turned to the General of the Croatian army, was that a regular thing that happened, or was that a special way of acting which was not something which ordinarily was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this was not usual and it wasn't unusual either. The letter we read out yesterday was written because of the way of thinking and the way of functioning of the municipal authorities of Travnik. It was in line with their thoughts. It's not that there was a procedure making it compulsory on them to do so or not to do so. Also, a similar letter could possibly have been written in other municipalities too. I don't know that. I cannot confirm that. But the most important thing is that this letter shows how independent a municipal authority is. That is to say, they circumvent the central authority of Herceg-Bosna. The central authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was paralysed, and they write a letter directly. I don't know what the effects were of that letter, but I know as far as officers are concerned, these officers never came and were never in the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Not officers of the Croatian army or soldiers of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I said on 16 October that you didn't know. You said that you didn't know whether there were officers there or not, and now you're saying that there were not any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I said that I know that there were not any of them in the command of the Operative Zone. And the HVO had three other operative zones, north-western Herzegovina, Southeast Herzegovina, and whether there were such officers there at that time I don't know. And I said why. Because from 1991 until the Washington Accords, I was not in a position to leave the enclave, and I never received this official information by way of fact. So I'm saying this for sure in terms of the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Let me now turn to Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I will put a few questions to you for clarification. I appreciate that you cannot answer yes or no to every question, but I shall try my best to ensure that you do not have too great of difficulty. Of course, if you cannot answer yes or no, then I shall understand. Now, let me take up a point mentioned by Judge Riad towards the end of his questioning. It concerns the letter dated 12th of April, 1993, which was sent by the municipality of Travnik, I think under the hand of Mr. Purvan to President Tudjman, requesting a form of military assistance, and I have listened to your answer. I want you to react to a slightly different aspect of the matter. Was the municipality likely to write such a letter unless the HVO military authorities had advised them that there was a need for military assistance from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this was not likely. You saw, Your Honour, that that letter did not even get into the command of the Operative Zone. This was an initiative taken by this municipal authority, because they were judging whether the officers were properly trained or not, and whether this or that thing was done, whatever it says there. So they did not receive from the municipality any orders from the military authorities or certainly not from the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your answer would be that HVO military authorities were not likely to have advised the municipality to make that request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's how I'd like us to proceed. Now, there was some evidence by you concerning an order issued by General Blaskic about confiscating weapons from Muslims and giving them to the HVO. I think that can be found at page 13.185 of the record, gentlemen. You also said that order was not carried out. Do you recall that branch of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. Does this perhaps pertain to lifting the state of alert -- raising the state of alert in December -- January 1993, when they are supposed to act with weapons as you just said, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It was on the 16th of January, 1993, and General Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- had a covering order. You remember that. And you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, Your Honour. So as far as this activity is concerned, this activity, which was ordered, it was ordered for the following reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not going into the reasons, General, I'm just asking if you remember your testimony on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You said that General Blaskic's order was not carried out. Do you recall your testimony to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order was not carried out because -- because -- because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the convey did not go. The convey did not go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, for three weeks now you've been asked to answer the questions very precisely. I would like to support Judge Shahabuddeen. He doesn't want to hear the reasons right now. Just answer the questions as he asks them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You said in another place that, however, General Blaskic was geared to carrying out superior orders very strictly. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, and that is the way General Blaskic acted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you report to General Petkovic on the fact that the orders issued by him, General Blaskic, had not been carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not inform General Petkovic about the case that I spoke of. And why not? What did I want to say? The convoys were not moving at the time when it was ordered to act in such and such a way with the convoys and to take away weapons, et cetera. There were no conveys because in Gornji Vakuf there was a cease-fire, and so this was signed quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: To return to his order to which you referred this morning, directing commanding officers to execute deserters. Do you recall your evidence to that effect? I do not wish to spell it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I remember. That is to say to execute those who leave the front-line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that that order was not intended to be carried out and was not, in fact, carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I ask you this question: If you were a local commander who received that order, would you understand that you were intended to carry it out or that you were not intended to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would understand it to have it carried out, but I would have read the order in its entirety. And a very important point in this order is point 2. That is to say, to read this in front of all the soldiers in line, so that all of them would be warned as to what would happen to them. So I would have analysed the entire order, not only one assignment therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good, General. Now, let me turn to General Blaskic's report to you of his discovery in Zenica that people had been killed in Ahmici. You remember him saying that General Merdan was, in effect, distressed by the circumstance that 500 civilians had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, Mr. President, that is what it says in the report. And as regards the figure, I cannot dwell on that because I do not know whether it is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. His statement was that General Merdan was pretty worried about the 500 civilians killed in Vitez. For the purposes of the record and the convenience of the bar, the page is 12.504. Now, did General Blaskic say to you that that figure was incorrect or that General Merdan's statement was inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The General did not tell me that. I will try to quote him -- rather, remember what he told me. At the meeting in Zenica, I got information that there is a large number of persons killed in Ahmici, and among them are civilians too. That is the only thing that the General told me. I do not know the exact losses, but I believe that not that many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to these ammunition factories, if I may refer to them that way for short. There was one in Vitez, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that was a factory of explosives, and in Konjic there was an ammunition factory, so these were explosives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about this this morning. You said that ABiH had a triple aim, and one of the three aims was that the ABiH wished to take over possession of these ammunition factories. I'm referring to that part of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you were in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was the HVO likely to allow the ABiH to capture these ammunition factories, or was it more likely that the HVO would have destroyed these factories before the ABiH could have taken them over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the attack took place, the attack on this factory, because of the substance and the programme of production that this factory had, had there been an explosion of this kind the entire town of Vitez would have been jeopardised. So if it so happened that all the raw materials and everything that was in that factory was blown up, the town of Vitez would have suffered a catastrophe. That is to say, in a big radius, the town and the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So those the catastrophic possible consequences, I gather from you that the HVO, if it lost, would have preferred not to destroy the factories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what at that time the commander of the Operative Zone would have decided, but I think he could not decide on his own what he would do with the factory in a situation in which the BH army would have broken our lines and come into a position to take the factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let's turn a little to the burning of houses. I think the gist of your evidence was that yes, houses were burnt, but all such burning that occurred occurred within the framework of a military conflict. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly, yes. As far as the burning of houses is concerned, I said the following: That the burning of houses happened during the fighting, and that it happened after the fighting when there was no combat action in the way which I explained. That is to say, secretly during the night and under different circumstances, not to explain all the examples that I ever cited. So if Croatian houses are burning in the territory which is under BH army control, there will certainly be someone who will set fire to Muslim Bosniak houses. Or if Muslim Bosniak houses were burning on territory that was under HVO control, it is certain that Croatian houses under territory controlled by the BH army would be ablaze.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us take a hypothetical case like this. Muslims desire to evict and expel Croats from a Croat occupied village. The Muslims attack the Croat village, the Croats resist, a conflict ensues, and Croat houses are burnt. Would it be your position that those houses were burnt because of a military conflict or because of an original intention to evict the Croats from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, neither one nor the other. Allegation can not be taken explicitly as such for certain reasons. I said that houses were burning as a consequence of combat action, that is one thing. And they were burning for the reasons I mentioned. I could not assert that they were burning for the reasons that you mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You remember that document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 510, the one which said -- I wonder if you could be shown it. Mr. Registrar, could he be shown it? You remember there was some argument about a phrase which occurred in the passage, "The Bukovci village must be taken by nightfall on condition that we burn anything standing in our way." That's only for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember, Your Honour, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, General, how would a commanding officer in the field, who received this document, understand that instruction? Would he understand it as meaning -- understand it as meaning that he was required to burn anything standing in his way, or would he not so understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case I would not understand it in that way. Why? Mr. President, Your Honours, the assignment was to disarm the soldiers of the BH army in those villages, and if that did not happen, if they did not surrender their weapons voluntarily, then they would be threatened in this way. So the main thing to be done was to disarm them, and then the rest was by way of a threat. When one studies an order, one has to understand what is the priority task, and what are the additional tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand, General. Now, I want you to bear in mind the map that Mr. Nobilo very kindly put up on the easel, the green map, and have it in mind as I speak to you. Certain preparatory and combat orders had been issued by General Blaskic on the 15th and, I believe, on the morning of the 16th. Would I be right in thinking that the orientation there was this: That the various elements of the HVO, including the Military Police, would be looking in the direction of the Nadioci, Ahmici, Sivrino, Pirici axis; is that correct? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that was not stated in the orders. If need be, I shall clarify all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I know it wasn't stated. I'm asking you whether as a matter of fact those elements of the HVO military would be oriented in the direction of the Nadioci, Ahmici, Sivrino, Pirici axis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You tell me then what is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct from the preparatory order issued on the 15th what the tasks all the units had. I will stress the tasks of the forces shown on this particular map. The Military Police had its task to control the communication line. To control the communication line, not to attack any village. All the brigades had the task of blocking, that is to say control the Croatian villages. There is no movement of forces, no attack, but at 1.00 a.m., General Blaskic, I suppose, had received additional information related to the intentions of the army, and in the area of the Vitez municipality where the Vitez Brigade was deployed, and I'll show you this, it is this entire region here, and according to his knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you show us, as well, Ahmici in relation to the other areas? Where is Ahmici? That's Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I right that some of the orders issued by General Blaskic at around this time mentioned that the army of the ABiH was occupying Ahmici or about to occupy the Ahmici area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The orders of General Blaskic to -- of which you mean do not say that. Ahmici was not occupied. There were BH army units there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. If independent criminal elements infiltrated at that time and entered Ahmici, would the various elements of the HVO have been in a position to detect that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand you when you say "elements". You mean elements of the HVO or elements of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. I wonder if I may have mixed my expressions up. Let me go again. If independent criminal elements had infiltrated at that time into the Ahmici area, would the various elements of the HVO have been in a position to detect that fact and to stop that intrusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they wouldn't be in a position to stop it in the village of Ahmici. You could reach Ahmici from Zenica without the HVO knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you reach Ahmici from the main road along which the Military Police of the HVO were strung out without the HVO becoming aware of the intrusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You couldn't get there, because Ahmici, the houses of Ahmici were along the road as well, along the edge of the road. They're very short distances, 20 metres, 30 metres. And I said in my testimony how the conflict on the road occurred. We saw the report that the commander of the Military Police said they were attacked in the Bungalow. All these facts, to this very day, I am -- have not thrown light on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Tell me something else. From where you were located in Vitez, could you hear any explosions coming from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there was fighting in the village of Ahmici and then -- then stronger explosions could be heard. But let me remind you that on the 16th, in the Vitez area, there were conflicts in the -- in places, Krucicia, Stari Vitez, Donja Rovna, Bare, Kuber, Ahmici, Krcevine, Grbavica and Jardoc. And if you recall, when I said that the civilian population had called us, the people said there was shooting from all sides, "We don't know what to do." And this was an appeal, and this was, in fact, fighting where there was detonation and the sound of explosion on all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I understand you, in effect, to be saying that the physical situation was too confusing for you to be able to locate precisely the direction from which any particular explosion was coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation, we cannot say that it was confusing, but I said that the forces of shelling from the BH army, from the town of Vitez, an all-out attack, that was a surprise to us, because in the orders dated the 15th, we expected sabotage activity by the BH army on the command posts, and that is why we blocked the villages. But we did not expect an all-out attack, the kind that occurred. And in a situation of this kind, the command in which I was, it was our need to see where the attack came from, whether you would be able to counter it and stop it and so on. And the command in which I was located, that was the key question, and every command would have given thought to these matters in a situation of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, when did you first hear on the media that certain dreadful things had occurred at Ahmici? When was the first time that you heard that on the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the media, but I heard about these events from my commander on the 20th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you also hear of them from the media, from the radio, the newspapers and so on, television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but at that time during the war, via the media, the public information media, there was an all-out propaganda being launched in the sense of saying who was responsible for the attack, who had attacked whom and the kind of events that were taking place, and it was really -- there was a mass of information put out and misinformation, I might say, so that when all this ended, and when I compared and analysed the information, I saw that half of the information put out was not correct. For example, the massacre at Kuber, that was not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I have no doubt you could give us a great number of details, but answer this question. Did the propaganda, or the information on the media, also include references to war crimes having been committed at Ahmici and to the possibility of a war crimes court being set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the media I believe that Ahmici was mentioned. And the war crimes court, as far as I remember, it was at that time in April, or perhaps March, the International Community did establish a war crimes court to deal with the crimes on the areas of the former Yugoslavia, I don't know exactly what date that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn a little to trench digging. I think you said that information came to you about trench digging. Did you recognise that information as referring to possible crimes against the international rules which applied to the conduct of warfare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That trenches were being dug and the line of defence set up, that was something I knew of, because we ordered the commanders of the units to see to those lines, because otherwise we wouldn't be able to defend ourselves. However, to engage civilians to set up this line, I said how this was done. It happened that everybody who was not a soldier and carried a rifle in those one, two or three days, how far it took to set up the line, was engaged via a work duty to perform those tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me read your testimony at page 13.262. Mr. Prosecutor asked you this question: "Were those prisoners taken out to dig trenches on front-lines and elsewhere?" Answer: "I cannot confirm that, although the information that I have personally received, as I worked with my colleagues, said that there were such things; but this was never ordered by the commander of the Operational Zone." Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you in general; you received some information on the subject. Did you think this was a sufficiently important matter for to you mention to General Blaskic? If so, did you mention it to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That information which reached me in the way in which I stated, it came after the event, after it had happened, because that activity took place in the space of two or three days, in the conflicts in Busovaca, in January, and in the conflicts in Vitez on the 16th, so that, it was something that had already been done and passed. And I will just remind you of General Blaskic's order, where, on the basis of an order from the commander of the main staff, he asked the commander of the units to give them the names of individuals who acted in that way. So, I did not have the information at the time when this occurred on the 16th or the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The answer is that, for one reason or another, you did not relay to General Blaskic the information which you had received about trench digging by prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information that I received in the way that I received it, I did not relate to General Blaskic. This information did not reach me via the operative report. It was an information, some information that reached me through what people were saying in town, by word of mouth, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little bit about logistical cooperation between the Serb military and the Croat military, the HVO. I gather from what you say the cooperation was limited to logistic matters and to only in some places; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this Trial Chamber what was your understanding of the basis on which that cooperation was being done? What was the basis of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basis, in my opinion, and this is really my own personal opinion, the basis for that cooperation was necessity, or dire need of the HVO units acting in the Kiseljak area and the enclave and the Zepce area in the enclave, because had they not received logistic material via the territory of Republika Srpska, they would have nothing to defend themselves with. And I felt this best in the encirclement in the Lasva Valley. It was our luck that along with the explosives factory, we were in fact defending ourselves in that way, and with that we were able to replace at least partially what we lacked. And so, it was dire need, it was necessity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether General Blaskic knew of this limited cooperation based on necessity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't confirm that but I suppose he could have known about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, think this was a sufficiently strange or important matter to mention to General Blaskic, I mean cooperation between the HVO and an active enemy in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours, it is strange, but it testifies to the character of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You see, on the one hand you have HVO units in enclaves, and on the other hand the army cooperating, also on logistic matters, this is something that is very difficult to explain, both the cause and effects of that and the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn to women and children being made to stand in the streets and then being taken into a building next to Mr. Cerkez's building. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If a shell fell on the part of the building occupied by Mr. Cerkez, could the blast affect the women and children in the adjoining part of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because that building where the civilians were placed was constructively speaking the strongest building in Vitez, and Vitez as a town had no shelter, no standard shelters for civilians in the case of shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I ask you a supplementary question on that. Suppose the enemy wanted to shell Mr. Cerkez; do you, as a military man, estimate that there might have been a risk of the shell either falling on the part of the building occupied by the women or children, or falling hard nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was possible. However, if you allow me, Your Honour, the town of Vitez is a small area. It would have been a greater tragedy had those civilians remained outside in the streets. And practically speaking, we had nowhere to put those people, because there was fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about the HV symbols which some elements of the military were wearing. I gather from what you said that some Croats in Herzeg-Bosna went over to help the military in Croatia, and they came back wearing Croatian insignia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because the war in Croatia began before it began in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you, then, have expected that in your hour of need the Croatian military or elements of the Croatian military would then come over to the Lasva Valley to help the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could have expected everything, but I know what actually happened. In the Lasva Valley, there was no Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, from your evidence and the evidence of others who testified for the Defence, the picture I have received is that the HVO was out numbered and under equipped in relation to the ABiH; do you subscribe to that view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I subscribe to that view; but I also confirm that for the units of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, I know the situation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In those circumstances, if military elements from Croatia had come over to help you, to help the HVO, would the HVO have welcomed that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you are in a situation, in the kind of situation that we were in, and that is, you have the encirclement there, you can see it, everybody giving you assistance would be welcomed. Because it was truly a situation where it was difficult to find a way out, and it was a struggle for survival, or to go under. Because we saw the fate of the soldiers and civilians in those places which were not defended, both Travnik, Kakanj, Vares, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question or two about this military concept of unity of command or unity of control. Is it unity of control you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a function of control it is not unity, it is -- so, unity is command, which implies subordination, responsibility and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you remember that on the ABiH side it was the 7th Muslim Brigade and the HVO were not too sure how closely connected the 7th Muslim Brigade was to the ABiH, or whether it was on the control under the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put it in pieces to you, then. Do you remember speaking about the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And you remember saying something to us to the effect that the 7th Muslim Brigade might not have been fully under the control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that. I said that. Just a bit, just a minute, please. I said that we were not sure whether the 3rd Corps controlled the 7th Brigade, not the army as an army. If not the 3rd Corps, then perhaps the general staff had control over them, so the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I accept that qualification. I'm grateful to you for it. Nevertheless, the HVO authorities wrote to the 3rd Corps in respect of things being done by the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we did send such a letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would you say, to use the language of Mr. Nobilo, that the proposition to be deduced from that is that you associated unity of command with exclusivity of command, that is, there could be no parallel and independent force existing in the same side, it all had to be brought under one single control; wasn't that your point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It would have been necessary and it could have functioned that way, but it did not. And I said how it had functioned. It was desirable, and that is what every commander would have wished for, that is to say, if he had forces on his territory and under his command, he would be the only one who would command them. But that was not the situation, neither with the army or the HVO. So, these were problems which were characteristic of the beginning of the organisation and set up both of the HVO and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I finally invite your attention to Exhibit 362, I think it's a Prosecutor's Exhibit 362, dated 24 April, 1993. Mr. Dubuisson, I hope I'm not misleading you, I better show you the document that I have. It's marked 362 in lead pencil. No? 24 April? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I think it's a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That solves the mystery. It is a Defence Exhibit. May I ask you a preliminary question like this, General? Would I be correct in supposing that in practically all armies there would be a tendency to have out of control elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not confirm that, in a state where there is rule of law that should not be the case. And in the situation that we had in Bosnia and Herzegovina, both the army and the HVO, this was possible, and this was practically an every day practice. It was reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What should not be is distinguishable from what could be. Now, if you look at this document, am I right that General Blaskic here is asserting a right of control over out of control elements? In paragraph 3 he says, "The individuals and groups who are completely out of control are to be arrested immediately." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see that, I see this paragraph, and it confirms that General Blaskic did not reconcile himself to this phenomenon, and he fought against such phenomena constantly. Practically, until the Washington Accords, he did not accept this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that. One last document is Defence 359, Defence document 359. Now, you see this document, like some others, was addressed to a number of elements, including military police 4th Battalion and Special Purposes Unit Vitezovi. Would you say, General Marin, that you would understand this document as a document displaying the exercise of authority by the commander who signed it over the military police and the Special Purposes Unit Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This is an operative order, how to behave on the ground, what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Now, look at paragraph 3, it says there, "Those who act in violation of this order are to be subject to the strictest measures in line with the rules on military discipline in HVO units." Wouldn't you understand that as being also addressed to the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but that would be carried out by their commander. That is to say, for a member of the Vitezovi, a disciplinary measure can be imposed only by the commander of Vitezovi, and not General Blaskic, for a member of the military police it is only a commander of the military police that can carry out this disciplinary action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you saying that the relationship was this: That General Blaskic could issue operational orders to the Vitezovi, but in case of non-compliance, he couldn't enforce them by imposing any sanctions, he had to refer the matter to other authorities? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we saw in the process of reaching such orders, the General, in order to prevent this from happening, always talked to the commander of the Vitezovi, and then when he agreed, he would send these orders in order to strengthen the organisation and command and to show that orders had to be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, he had the power to issue operational orders, but he didn't have the power, himself, to enforce them by imposing any sanctions of his own.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. I want to turn to my interpreter friends again, because it is now 5.45, we have gone beyond the time limit. You know, of course, the interpreters are going to be in court tomorrow morning, but we are going to resume at 2 o'clock. I have a few questions I would like to ask. Thanks to my colleagues, many of my own questions were already asked. I would like to turn to the interpreters and ask them whether we could go ten minutes or fifteen minutes longer and so finish with this testimony so that the Brigadier can go home and not have to wait until the day after tomorrow or tomorrow afternoon. Once again, I would like to thank the interpreters, and once again, I would express my appreciation. I will ask some very concluding questions. Brigadier, you have answered many questions asked by my colleagues. One asked, perhaps, was not really taken up over the many days that we have been meeting, that is the political aspect about everything that happened regarding the constitution of the Croatian defence community. Before I ask my question I would like to ask whether you agree on the premise. Do you remember this entire period between 1992 and January 1993 when a real state within the state had been constituted, there was a currency, there was an official journal, there were schools and rules of all types, and also very great propaganda from the political players of Herceg-Bosna which kindled that part of the population in Central Bosnia? Do you remember that? I don't know if you do, but perhaps you do. But do you agree that politicians assert a certain idea of the extension, the hegemony of the thoughts and ideas of a more extensive Croatian territory which might in fact cross, spill over into Bosnia and Herzegovina? Would you agree with that? Would you say that that existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I could not confirm what you have said. Everything I know about political developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the following: I know there was a paralysis of government in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the official, legally and legitimately, elected parliament fell apart, and it fell apart when the deputies of the Serb people left the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when they decided, when their political leadership decided to carry out an aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Brigadier, I'm not asking for your, for justifications, that's not the question. I simply wanted to know whether you would agree that there was the constitution in Herceg-Bosna, that there was an official journal, there was currency which was related to Croatian currency, there were changes in the teaching programmes, there was a kind of state within a state. I'm not asking whether that was justified or not, perhaps it was or was not, that's not the question. I want to know whether there was that period of intense propaganda which could have kindled the spirits through propaganda, through television? Did that exist, do you remember, and do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we saw that this question of all normative enactments did exist, the legislation, et cetera, as far as propaganda is concerned, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, all three sides did engage in some kind of propaganda, Mr. President. I really am not a member of any political party, I was never the member of any political party, and I'm not today, and I was never in a political body, and I don't know what kind of political decisions were made and what their objectives were. So, indeed, to give a yes or no answer to your question would be too arbitrary. I do not know enough in order to say it was so or it was not so. Because the truth is between yes and no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am very pleased that you answered that, because at least now I have an answer, that the truth is now down somewhere between yes and no. That's how you have often answered. But that was the not the question. At least you agree that at that period there was, at least on the Croatian side after the elections -- or on the Croatian Party that came out of the election, that there was a kind of heating up of public opinion against the Muslims with the constitution of a real -- let's not call it a State, but a kind of a political and administrative organisation. Do you like that term better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was a temporary set-up, administrative set-up, but I could not agree with you, Mr. President, that immediately after the elections there was unrest. It was after the aggression of the army of Republika Srpska against Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's when the problem started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, you always have the impression that you're going to be accused of something. I am assure that you the accused is sitting over there. We're trying to shed light on the subject, but you're always on the defensive. You don't have to be on the defensive. Try to relax a little bit. It seemed to me that when we saw a text which put into place a new -- I don't think we'd be going too far that there was a kind of constitution. Mr. Nobilo, I new this was the time you were going to come in. All right, but go quickly (sic) please for the interpreter's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. I know that it is not proper for me to interrupt the Presiding Judge, but perhaps it can be helpful if we move to a private session. This witness works where he works, and the people who created this are his bosses and so you have to appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Nobilo, that the witness, when he answered, puts himself to a justifying position. I haven't yet asked my question. I was only asking him whether he agreed that between November and February of 1993; through the documents, through school curriculum that had been changed, currency that was introduced, I suppose it's not General Marin who is the one who originated all of that. If the General feels accused, that's his own feeling. Let me finally get to my question that I want to ask. As far as you know, did the accused, through his personal opinions, participate or share, rather, the idea of the constitution of this entity, which we call Bosnian Croat, within that central part of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was he able to play a political role? You see, that is a question that has to do with the accused and not with you, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Blaskic did not have a political role. However, as commander of the Operative Zone, he certainly did have a certain significance, but that he had a political role or a political office, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, in your opinion, he had been appointed only because of his military qualifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know that is the way it was, because General Blaskic, may I remind you, Mr. President, came from Austria, from Austria, after he escaped from the former JNA, and he was appointed commander. I don't know whether he was a member of the HDZ ever. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is my question: Within the context of that time, could one imagine that the Croatian defence community would name one of the highest military officials right before the war was about to begin, could it appoint one of its military officials about whom they were not sure that he shared the political opinions of the political leaders of Herceg-Bosna? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I do not think that at that time when General Blaskic was appointed a man could be appointed to that office without being ready to shoulder the burden of defence, the defence of the territory and Croatian people. General Blaskic was appointed commander of the operative zone when there was fighting against the army of Republika Srpska, and when we held the front-line together with the BH army. That's when General Blaskic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In order to finish with that question, you consider that, first of all, General Blaskic did not have any political role in the first place, and in the second place, he believed that his military activities were to serve the Croatian people. Do we agree with those two theories? First proposal -- proposition, rather, is that he only played a military role, but the second proposition is that he put his military qualifications at the service of the Croatian people. You are the one who just said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I feel that I played the same kind of role too, and every officer in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't speak but you. Otherwise, Mr. Nobilo is going to get up and say we have to move into a private session. Don't speak about yourself. The question that I want to ask, and I'm going to change gears, at one point my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, was speaking, very strangely, the accused, who is Colonel Blaskic, speaks about the creation of this Tribunal, which proves that he was well-informed. And he emphasises in that order that what is happening, that is -- that certain types of atrocities that have been committed might allegedly be considered to be crimes, and you know that crimes -- the word "crime" was written with capital letters. Do you remember that? There were two orders. I think that those are Defence exhibits. One which the defence says now there's a Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I won't ask you whether the accused was concerned about those same issues before the establishment of the Tribunal, because that was not my question. But in a second order he said, let me remind you, that what might be considered atrocities could also be considered crimes in International Law. Therefore, my question is to know whether at any point the accused wrote to his superiors, informed his superiors about his doubts, about the questions he was asking himself about the crimes. For example, did he write to General Petkovic and say, "You know, I believe that there are crimes which may be being committed, and I think that's very serious." In your opinion, did he do that, or was that not part of your responsibilities and there would be no way for you to know so? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. President. General Blaskic, with regard to the problems he had, and, therefore, also the problems related to the non-functioning of the order system, he wrote about that to his superiors. However, his superiors could not help him with this either for two reasons. One is the physical separation that took place then, and the second was that the entire HVO functioned in a similar or perhaps exactly the same way in which the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia functions. There are several reports sent by General Blaskic to General Petkovic, where he sends him detailed information on how it was. That is to say, from a military point of view from the point of view of problems, needs and other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You remember that among other things, there is a report in which the accused says, "The winter is coming, it's going to be a very harsh winter, we don't have blankets, we don't have material, we don't have boots, because it's going to snow." Therefore, he was addressing himself to his superiors. Strategically speaking, you should know that because you were the number two operative person. My question is to know whether or not he drafted a report in which he said, "The war has begun, it's a horrible war, atrocities are being committed on all sides, but there are some which may have been committed by our people, they're crimes, what should we do? I have elements that are out of control." Did you speak about that together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We saw the report after the meeting with Stewart, that he wrote everything that was mentioned, and what the problems were. And there is a report from May, the month of May, after the cease-fire was signed, after the fighting in April. And the General writes to his superiors exactly the way military rules prescribe. And General Petkovic also attended meetings with General Blaskic in Zenica, and on the 21st in Bila. So in that way, together with Sefer Halilovic, the commander of the army, they were all practically familiar with what was discussed at that meeting. So the general did write about the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, he had the information. That's what you're saying to us right now. At least -- well, he had the information about what was going on. As regards violations of International Humanitarian Law, the accused had information, at least at the time, that there were meetings being held at the representative of the ECMM and UNPROFOR. He had information available to him. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Information? Yes. Yes. Information on the violation of those laws. It started on the 21st, and then Mr. Stewart on the 22nd, et cetera. Information on events, not about persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In the briefings, do you remember the accused having said, "I'm very worried. I'm going to send another message asking for help, expressing my distress. I'm going to send it to my superiors." Did he also give you instructions of that nature, or he was simply satisfied with having received the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that form -- I mean, that General Blaskic spoke in that form, that I do not recall, but I do know what he did in terms of improving the situation on the ground as much as possible, and I know what he wrote on the 25th or 26th to his superior in Mostar -- or, rather, in Posusje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: To finish with that point, one day, did the accused ever say to you, "I'm going to resign"? "I can't stay in this position." You heard my question. This is the very nature of great -- of people who are very, very -- of very high, important positions. I'm going back -- you've been saying to us for three weeks that his subordinates don't obey him, his superiors don't help him or he can't reach them. Did one day he say to you, "I've come from Vienna in Austria. I am a professional." You did say that. You know that you said that he was a professional. "I'm just simply going to resign." Do you remember his having said that once or twice, or not at all, or did it never come to his mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember, or rather, the General did not say this in front of me. However, I'm trying to go back to this situation and to the General's thinking. And I assert that a situation would have been even worse if the operative zone command was not headed by a person such as General Blaskic, and I say this with full responsibility. Because out of all of us, although he was not fully qualified for the job, he was certainly the most qualified officer amongst all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you my last question. During your long testimony, I have frequently had difficulties in distinguishing your specific responsibilities, because at one point you're number two of the staff, you have important responsibilities and very often you said that you weren't there, you didn't attend the proper briefing, or that you were absent, or that you were doing something else. I have to confess this to you, this was somewhat problematic for me. With a bit of time now, I want to ask you one question only. General Blaskic was, therefore, the highest military authority in Central Bosnia for the 3rd Operative Zone. We do agree to that; do we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that he fully exercised his responsibility. I can ask the question differently. Would you agree with me if I said that he fully carried out his responsibilities as the chief of the Operative Zone in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. General Blaskic tried and strived for ensuring the carrying out of his post as it was required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're very close to him, you were very close to him every day. Here is my question: At any given point during that time of command and war, in the application of -- to international humanitarian law, do you believe that the accused may have made some mistakes either as regards the organisation of his troops, or in the information of his superiors, or in the reports that he might have given to UNPROFOR? Do you remember it possible that he made mistakes, or do you think that he made no mistakes at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my personal judgement I believe that General Blaskic did everything that was possible during 1993 as commander of the Operative Zone. Truth to tell, after such actions we still have the situation as it was in the war between the units of the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I think that if there are no further questions, first of all, the Tribunal would like to thank you, Brigadier Marin. You came -- I know you have important responsibilities in your country. You came for a few days at first, and then, as it turned out, for several weeks. The Tribunal is grateful to you for having answered its very long questions and the questions of the Judges, and thanks to the availability of our interpreters, you will not have to come back tomorrow and the Tribunal wishes you God speed when you return home and resume your responsibilities. Once again I would like to thank the interpreters. I think at 9.30 -- no? I was thinking about the interpreters. I'll see the interpreters at 9.30. Mr. Hayman, I didn't make a mistake there. I know that you're very vigilant, but here this vigilance was the not quite right. Now, we'll see the interpreters at 9.30, because I know -- and I know that they're tired, and we have to resume. However, both the Defence and the accused -- the Prosecution and the accused we'll see at 2.00 tomorrow afternoon. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You too, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of October, 1998 at 2.00 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
